scenes.heading: What pH measures
scenes.narration: Every water based solution you meet contains hydrogen ions, and the pH value records how crowded with those particular hydrogen ions a given solution really happens to be.

scenes.heading: The zero to fourteen scale
scenes.narration: The familiar scale runs from 0 all the way up to 14. Pure water sits exactly at 7, and chemists have agreed to call that midpoint neutral.

scenes.heading: The acidic side
scenes.narration: Readings below 7 mean that the solution counts as acidic. Lemon juice sits near 2 and tastes sharp, while stomach acid is lower still at roughly 1.

scenes.heading: The basic side
scenes.narration: Readings above 7 mean the solution is basic, which is also called alkaline. Soapy water sits near 10 and feels slippery, while household bleach lands close to 13.

scenes.heading: Each step multiplies tenfold
scenes.narration: The scale is logarithmic, so every single step along it changes the hydrogen ion concentration by 10 times. Two steps together therefore mean a full hundredfold jump.

scenes.heading: Putting it together
scenes.narration: So pH counts hydrogen ions on a logarithmic scale where 7 is neutral, anything lower counts as acidic, and anything higher counts as basic or alkaline instead.
